meta.title: Stepwise runs — one step, one run, one verdict
meta.description: The plan becomes the execution unit: each step gets its own generated prompt and its own run, verified against that step's own criteria before the next starts. A step that needs earlier work reopens it as rev_n and resumes. The mechanism lives in the CORE and both surfaces drive it — the native strip simply, the RFX planner with every control exposed.

frames.label: 2 · Drive — the new part: who decides what runs next
3 · Run — one step, start to verdict

nodes.label: The user's prompt
nodes.note: TODAY this same text is injected into every iteration of one long run, so the model must hold the whole task in mind at once and is trusted to touch each point on its own. In the new design it is used ONCE, to plan.

nodes.label: Step criteria
nodes.sublabel: NEW · each step declares a check that CAN FAIL
nodes.note:
commit_plan gains a `verify` field per step: the concrete observation that proves the step done. Without it there is nothing to verify against and "done" falls back to guessing from disk — the bug in run-dataflow.

The model writes its own exam, so the SHAPE is constrained rather than the wording trusted (decided 2026-09-04). A verify must be one of three runnable forms:
  • a check_page eval that returns a boolean
  • a command whose exit code decides it
  • a file that must contain a named symbol

Existence-only checks are REJECTED at commit time, the way the plan gate already rejects a prose plan — "index.html exists" is the disk guess wearing a costume.

And a criterion can be impossible as easily as it can be lazy: the car run's own eval could never pass under file:// however correct the page was. So a step whose verify never passes gets a small budget, then hands back with the evidence. An unpassable check costs one step, never the task.

nodes.label: Step supervisor
nodes.sublabel: NEW · owns the cursor: which step, which revision, what next
nodes.note:
The piece that does not exist today. It holds the step cursor, starts one run per step, reads each verdict and decides: advance, retry this step, or reopen an earlier one. It never writes code itself — it only decides what the next run is asked to do.

It is also the natural home for the turn budget: a stall or a loop ends THIS step's run, not the whole task, so the other steps still get their chance.

nodes.label: Step prompt writer
nodes.sublabel: NEW · the model writes the prompt for the next run
nodes.note:
Given the plan, the step, and what earlier steps actually produced, the model writes the prompt for this step's run: what to build, which files, what must be true at the end. Generated, never templated — a hardcoded prompt cannot know that step 2 renamed a function step 3 depends on.

Cheap: one short call per step, against a plan that is already committed.

nodes.label: Revision decider
nodes.sublabel: NEW · reopen an earlier step as rev_n · cap 2 · re-verify downstream
nodes.note:
When a run reports that an EARLIER step is wrong or incomplete, the supervisor opens a revision run for that step — rev_2, rev_3 — with the new context explaining what is needed and why. When it passes, the cursor returns to where it left off. The model asks for this via a `needs_step` field on the verdict; the harness does not guess.

TWO RULES stop it looping, decided 2026-09-04:

1. CAP. Two revisions per step. The third request hands back to the user with every verdict on record, rather than spending the task on one disputed file.

2. RE-VERIFY DOWNSTREAM. A revision can invalidate a later step that was verified against the old file. After any revision, re-run the verify of every later step that shares a file with the revised one. Cheap — it is the declared check, not a new run — and it catches the silent breakage. If the same PAIR of steps fails twice, that is a genuine disagreement about the design: hand back with both verdicts instead of trying a third time.

nodes.label: Step run
nodes.sublabel: one step · its own generated prompt · its own iteration budget
nodes.note: The existing agent loop, scoped. Same tools, same guards, but the turn is ONE step: it starts with the step's prompt, ends when the step verifies or the budget runs out. Failures stop a step, not the task.

nodes.label: Step verify
nodes.sublabel: run the step's own criteria · pass / fail, with evidence
nodes.note: Runs what the step declared: the eval, the command, the file check. The verdict is an observation, not the model's opinion that it is finished.

nodes.label: checkpoint event
nodes.sublabel: step N, rev R — passed / failed, and the evidence
nodes.note:
Written by the supervisor when a run ends, per step and revision. This is the event BuildReportAt already prefers and has never once received, which is why status is currently guessed from disk.

Once these exist, "done" means the step's own check was observed to pass.

nodes.label: events.jsonl
nodes.sublabel: one log · plan, runs, checkpoints, revisions

nodes.label: GET /report + /state
nodes.sublabel: status now comes from checkpoints, not from disk

nodes.label: Native plan strip
nodes.sublabel: SIMPLE surface · steps, which one is running, pass/fail · no knobs
nodes.note:
What a user gets with no RFX pack installed. Shows the plan the moment it commits, marks the running step, shows each verdict as it lands, and offers ONE action: continue after a hand-back. Everything else is automatic.

It must not be a second implementation of the loop — it renders core state and nothing more.

nodes.label: RFX Planner panel
nodes.sublabel: ADVANCED surface · per-step run, re-run, revise, select, auto-continue
nodes.note:
~/.crv/rfx/planner/ui/panel.html. Already drives steps today, but ONLY by writing English prompts through rfx.turn() ("Continue the committed plan: do step 3 only, then stop and report") and inferring status from which files exist. It is a smart panel compensating for a core that has no step cursor.

When the supervisor exists, the panel stops composing prompts and starts calling it: run step N, re-run with revision, set auto-continue. Same buttons, real semantics — and its own comment already says the intelligence belongs in cerveau, not the panel.

flags.title: The panel drives steps by writing English, which is why the plan is decoration
flags.note: Today the planner's step buttons build a sentence and post it as a normal autopilot turn: "Continue the committed plan: do step 3 (Cameras + UI) only, then stop and report." The core has no idea a step was requested. It gets a prompt like any other, so nothing binds the run to step 3, nothing verifies step 3, and no checkpoint is written. The panel then infers status from which declared files exist — the same disk guess as the report.\n\nThat is the whole decoration problem in one place: a surface that looks like it controls execution, sitting on a core with no concept of a step. The panel's own comment ("deliberately dumb, the intelligence is cerveau's") describes the intent; the code cannot honour it because there is nothing in the core to be intelligent.
flags.fix: Give the core the step semantics (supervisor + step control API), then change the panel's kick() from composing prose to calling run-step {step, rev}. The buttons stay; what they mean becomes real. Keep the panel's scenario rules (auto-continue, pause on failure) as UI policy — those are genuinely presentation, unlike prompt-writing.

ports.shape: POST run-step {step, rev?} · POST auto {on} · GET plan-state

nodes.label: Step control API
nodes.sublabel: NEW · the one way to drive a plan · both surfaces call it
nodes.note:
One contract so the two surfaces cannot drift apart. The native strip uses a slice of it (continue after hand-back); the planner uses all of it (run one step, re-run, revise, select a subset, auto-continue).

The RFX bridge gains a matching capability so a sandboxed panel can call it without composing prompts.
